interest: This file provides valuable insight into the legal and diplomatic maneuvering between the United States and Japan during the drafting of the 1935 Philippine Constitution. It reveals that the State Department's inquiry into Article 5 of the Japanese Mining Law and other restrictions on foreign exploitation of natural resources was directly linked to Japanese diplomatic protests or suggested modifications regarding resource-nationalism clauses in the Philippine draft constitution. The records concisely illustrate how the U.S. government researched Japanese domestic statutes—including mining prohibitions, territorial fishing rights, and state subsidies—to assess reciprocity and counter Japanese objections to foreign-ownership restrictions in the emerging Philippine Commonwealth.
overview: This file comprises State Department telegrams, an internal research memorandum, and a cross-reference sheet from March 1935 concerning legal restrictions on foreign nationals developing or exploiting natural resources in Japan. Prompted by Japanese government representations regarding the draft constitution of the Philippine Islands, Secretary of State Cordell Hull instructed the American Embassy in Tokyo to report on Article 5 of the Japanese Mining Law and any other statutory prohibitions against foreign economic exploitation. Far Eastern Affairs staff noted legal restrictions on mining, hunting, and fishing, while Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reported that aside from the mining statute and laws limiting subsidies to Japanese subjects, no other specific legal restrictions barred foreign business activities in Japan.

subfiles.about: Inquiry to the Tokyo Embassy regarding Japanese legal provisions restricting the development of natural resources by foreign nationals.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull inquires of the American Embassy in Tokyo regarding Article 5 of the Japanese Mining Law. Hull asks whether any other legal provisions prohibit or restrict foreign nationals from exploiting or developing Japan's natural resources. He requests that the embassy telegraph translations of any pertinent statutory provisions.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Department of State to Tokyo Embassy regarding restrictions on foreign exploitation of natural resources

subfiles.about: Internal research note quoting Japanese mining law and legal commentary on alien rights regarding natural resources and territorial waters.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State Far Eastern Affairs Division memorandum quotes Article V of the Mining Law of Japan, noting that only Japanese subjects or duly formed juridical persons may acquire mining rights. It additionally cites J. E. De Becker's treatise on international private law regarding alien exclusions from fishing or hunting in Japan's territorial waters.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Japanese Mining Law and alien rights

subfiles.about: Report from Ambassador Grew on legal restrictions affecting foreign business enterprises and natural resource development in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew replies to the Department's inquiry concerning legal restrictions on foreigners. He reports that apart from the mining law, individual subsidy laws restrict benefits strictly to Japanese subjects. He concludes that there appear to be no other specific legal restrictions on foreign business activities in Japan.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ambassador Grew to Secretary of State regarding legal restrictions on foreigners

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet linking inquiries on Japanese natural resource laws to Japanese government proposals regarding the Philippine draft constitution.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references telegram 42 of March 15, 1935, filed under decimal file 811B.011/15. It explicitly links the inquiries regarding Japanese statutory restrictions on foreign resource exploitation to Japanese government suggestions for modifying the draft constitution of the Philippine Islands.
subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet regarding natural resource inquiries and the Philippine draft constitution
